standard_text: Select, create, and interpret graphical representations of numerical data, including line plots, histograms, and box plots.

progression.narrative: 6.DS.1 makes three demands, in its own words: SELECT, CREATE, and INTERPRET graphical representations of numerical data. The arc follows those verbs. First a student must know what each display is FOR -- dot plots show every value, histograms count values in equal intervals, box plots show a five-number summary -- so they can select the right one (S1). Selection only means something if the student can then read what a display says: the value on the axis versus the count in the stack or bar (S2). Creating comes next (S3), because building a plot -- an honest number line, one X per value, one interval per value -- is where the reading rules become physical. Interpretation then deepens in two steps: judging statements about a display using median, range, IQR, and quartile percentages (S4), and computing the five-number summary itself so a student can build or verify a box plot from raw data, with the Indiana convention that Q1 and Q3 exclude the median (S5). The standard tops out where ILEARN's Above-Proficiency items live: drawing a conclusion from one or two displays and defending it with values cited as evidence (S6). Underneath it all sit two foundations -- finding a median and range of a tiny ordered set (F1), and counting how often a value occurs (F2) -- because every display in this standard is just those two acts drawn as a picture.

steps.rationale: The standard's first verb. Choosing among dot plot, histogram, and box plot forces the student to know what each display shows -- the conceptual map every later skill navigates.

Interpretation begins with a single honest read: the value lives on the axis, the frequency lives in the stack or bar, and the median lives on the line inside the box. Nothing downstream works if these two roles swap.

The standard's second verb. Building a plot -- full number line, one X per value, equal intervals -- turns the reading rules into decisions the student must make, and exposes the compressed-axis error that silent reading never would.

The At-Proficiency demand: judge statements about a display. Median, range, IQR, and quartile percentages must each be pulled from the correct part of the plot -- a bar height is a count, never a data value.

Connecting raw data to its box plot requires computing the five-number summary with the spec's convention (Q1/Q3 exclude the median). This is what lets a student verify which plot represents a data set instead of guessing.
The Above-Proficiency demand: make a claim about (or across) displays and support it with cited values. Every prior skill supplies the evidence; this one teaches what counts as evidence.

skills.name: Find the median and range of a small ordered data set

prerequisite_skill.description: Order whole numbers and find the middle value and the spread of a small data set.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Put 9, 2, 6 in order from least to greatest. Which number is in the middle?

skills.i_do_script: Watch me find the median of 3, 9, 5. First I put the numbers in order: 3, 5, 9. The median is the middle number after ordering, so the median is 5 -- not 9, even though 9 was in the middle before I ordered. The range is a different question: biggest minus smallest, 9 - 3 = 6.

canonical_error.pattern: Finds the 'middle number' of the list as written, without ordering the data first.
canonical_error.example: For the data 9, 2, 6, the student says the median is 2 because 2 sits in the middle of the list.
canonical_error.why: The student treats 'median = middle' as a position on the page instead of a position in the ORDERED data. Ordering is the invisible first step, and skipping it makes every median wrong except by luck.

redirect_script.stop: Hold on -- did we put the numbers in order first?
redirect_script.prompt: Rewrite the data from least to greatest before you look for the middle. Cross off one number from each end, back and forth, until one number (or two) is left in the middle.
redirect_script.praise: You ordered first -- that's exactly what makes the median trustworthy.

skills.item_template: A list of 3-5 whole numbers (sometimes out of order). Student finds the median or the range. NR, no choices -- short stems suitable for fluency sprints.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: Find the median and range of 9, 2, 6.
Before we hunt for the middle, is this list in order from least to greatest?
Rewrite it in order for me. What do you get?
If the student says the median is 2 (the middle of the UNORDERED list), stop and ask: 'Is 2 really in the middle of these values, or just in the middle of the page?' Have them order first: 2, 6, 9.
Now cross off the smallest and the largest. What's left?
That leftover number, 6, is the median. Median always means the middle of the ORDERED data.
Range is a different job: biggest minus smallest. What is 9 - 2?
So median 6, range 7. Two different questions, two different answers.

skills.name: Count how often each value appears in a data set

prerequisite_skill.description: Count occurrences of a value in a list and identify the smallest and largest values.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: In the list 4, 6, 4, 7, 4 -- how many times does 4 appear?

skills.i_do_script: Watch me count how many 4s are in the data 4, 6, 4, 7, 4. I touch each number and make a tally every time I see a 4: tally, skip, tally, skip, tally. Three tallies, so 4 appears three times. Every dot plot, histogram, and box plot starts with counting like this, so we count every copy -- not just 'yes, a 4 is in there.'

canonical_error.pattern: Counts whether a value appears instead of how many times it appears -- repeats get collapsed to one.
canonical_error.example: For the data 4, 6, 4, 7, 4, the student says 4 appears '1 time' because '4 is one number.'
canonical_error.why: The student is thinking about the value as a single object instead of counting occurrences. Frequency -- the height of every stack and bar they'll ever read -- is exactly this count, so collapsing repeats breaks every display downstream.

redirect_script.stop: Wait -- let's touch and count each one.
redirect_script.prompt: Put your finger on each number in the list one at a time and make a tally mark every time you land on the value we're counting. How many tallies did you make?
redirect_script.praise: You counted every copy -- that count is what data displays are built from.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: Data: 5, 1, 5, 5, 2, 5. How many 5s?
Before you answer -- are we asking whether 5 is in the list, or how many TIMES 5 is in the list?
Those are different questions. Displays are built from 'how many times' -- that's called the frequency.
Touch each number one at a time. Make a tally every time you land on a 5. Go.
If the student answers 1 ('there's a 5 in there'), have them physically touch-count with tallies. If they answer 6, they counted every value -- reread the question together.
How many tallies did you make?
Four. On a dot plot, that would be a stack of 4 Xs above the number 5. Counting repeats IS making a data display.
Quick check: in 8, 3, 6, 3, 3 -- how many 3s?

skills.name: Select the appropriate display for a numerical data set
skills.i_do_script: Each display answers a different question. If I want to see EVERY individual value -- like 12 quiz scores with repeats -- I choose a dot plot (line plot). If my data comes in intervals -- like wages of $500-$600, $600-$700 -- I choose a histogram, because histograms group data into equal intervals. If I only care about the summary -- median, quartiles, minimum, maximum -- I choose a box plot. I ask 'what do I want to SEE?' before I pick.

canonical_error.pattern: Picks a bar graph (or circle graph) for numerical data because 'bars show numbers.'
canonical_error.example: For 20 race times grouped into intervals, the student picks 'bar graph' instead of 'histogram.'
canonical_error.why: The student hasn't separated CATEGORIES (favorite colors, pet types) from NUMERICAL data (times, heights). Bar graphs compare labeled categories; histograms cover a numerical scale with equal intervals. Without that distinction, every choice looks interchangeable.

redirect_script.stop: Wait -- is this data categories or numbers?
redirect_script.prompt: Ask two questions: (1) Are the data values NUMBERS on a scale, or category labels? (2) Do I want to see every value (dot plot), values grouped in intervals (histogram), or just the five-number summary (box plot)? Underline the words in the problem that answer question 2.
redirect_script.praise: You matched the display to what the data needs to show -- that's the whole skill.

skills.item_template: A described data set (7 or fewer values, whole numbers, sometimes grouped in intervals) plus a purpose ('see every value,' 'show how many in each interval,' 'show only the summary'). Student picks the best display. MC with 4 choices; other displays (bar graph, circle graph, stem-and-leaf) appear only as distractors.

sample_items.stem: A gym lists members' ages in intervals: 10-19, 20-29, 30-39, 40-49, with a count for each interval. Which graphical representation would best display this data?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Bar graph baits the categories-vs-intervals confusion; line plot would need individual values, which the intervals hide; box plot needs the five-number summary.

sample_items.stem: A teacher records each of 12 students' exact quiz scores (out of 10), including repeats, and wants a display that shows every individual score. Which display is most appropriate?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Histogram groups scores into intervals and hides individual values; box plot shows only the summary; circle graph shows parts of a whole, not numerical values.

sample_items.stem: A coach wants a display that shows only the median, the quartiles, and the minimum and maximum of her runners' race times. Which display should she choose?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Line plot shows every value instead of the summary; bar graph is for categories; circle graph shows parts of a whole.

sample_items.stem: Six students report how many pets they have: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 3. A student wants to see each value and how often it repeats. Which display is most appropriate?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Box plot hides individual values; circle graph is for parts of a whole; stem-and-leaf is a distractor display outside this standard's focus.

sample_items.stem: A scientist has 200 plant heights and wants to show how many plants fall in each 5 cm interval. Which display is most appropriate?
sample_items.distractor_logic: A line plot with 200 dots is unreadable; bar graph baits the categories confusion; circle graph shows parts of a whole.

vocabulary.definition: A number line with an X or dot stacked above each data value -- shows every individual value.
Bars over equal numerical intervals; each bar's height counts how many values land in that interval.
A display built from five numbers -- minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum -- that shows the summary, not individual values.
Any picture of data, like a dot plot, histogram, or box plot.

worked_example_script.text: Write: 'A gym lists members' ages in intervals: 10-19, 20-29, 30-39, 40-49, with a count for each interval. Which graphical representation would best display this data?' List the choices: line plot, bar graph, box plot, histogram.
First: is this data made of numbers on a scale, or category labels like favorite color?
Second: are these ages already grouped into equal intervals, or is it a list of each member's exact age?

If the student says 'bar graph, because bars show numbers,' pause. Ask: 'Bar graphs compare separate CATEGORIES like soccer vs. tennis. Are 10-19 and 20-29 categories, or equal chunks of one number line?'
Equal chunks of a number line is exactly what a histogram shows -- one bar per interval, bar height = how many members land in that age range.
Could a dot plot work here? What would we need that the interval counts don't give us?
Right -- a dot plot needs each member's exact age, but we only have interval counts. So a histogram it is.
The answer is a histogram: bars over the equal age intervals, each height counting the members in that range.

practice_problems.stem: Why would a dot plot be a poor choice for 500 values that range from 0 to 1000? What display works better, and why?

skills.name: Read values and frequencies from dot plots, histograms, and box plots
skills.i_do_script: On a dot plot, every question has two ingredients: the VALUE on the number line, and the COUNT of dots stacked above it. If the tallest stack is 3 dots above the number 5, then '5' is the value and '3' is how many. Watch me answer 'How many students read 5 books?' -- I find 5 on the line first, then count up the stack: 3. I never let the stack height and the axis number trade places.

canonical_error.pattern: Swaps the dot count and the axis value -- reports the number of dots when asked for the value, or the value when asked for the count.
canonical_error.example: The tallest stack is 3 dots above the number 4, and the student says 'the most common value is 3.'
canonical_error.why: The student reads the stack height as if it were the data value. A dot plot encodes two different numbers at every position -- the value (horizontal axis) and the frequency (dots) -- and until those roles are pinned down, every read is a coin flip. The same confusion reads a histogram bar's height as a data value.

redirect_script.stop: Hold on -- is that the value, or the count of dots?
redirect_script.prompt: Put one finger on the number line and say 'this is the VALUE.' Then walk your finger up the stack counting dots and say 'this is HOW MANY.' Now reread the question -- which of the two is it asking for?
redirect_script.praise: You kept the axis number and the dot count in their own jobs -- perfect read.

The question names a number of books -- the value 5. Where do we find 5: down in the dots, or on the number line? Put a finger on it.
Now walk your finger up the stack above 5. What is each X worth, and how many are stacked there?
Each X is one student, so the height of the stack is the frequency -- how many students. Three Xs means three students.

Now ask 'which number of books is the MOST common?' If the student answers '3' (the stack height), stop them: 'Three is how MANY -- that's the count. Read the number on the LINE under that tallest stack.' The most common value is 5; the count 3 and the value 5 must never trade jobs.
Back to our question -- say the whole sentence: how many students read exactly 5 books?
Three students read exactly 5 books. The value 5 lives on the line; the count 3 lives in the stack. The answer is 3.

skills.name: Create a dot plot or histogram from a numerical data set
skills.i_do_script: Watch me build a dot plot for the data 2, 3, 3, 5. First I draw a number line that covers EVERY value from the minimum to the maximum -- 2, 3, 4, 5 -- even 4, which has no data, because the spacing has to stay honest. Then one X per data value: one X above 2, two Xs above 3, none above 4, one X above 5. Four values in the data, four Xs on the plot -- I always count to check.

canonical_error.pattern: Compresses the number line by skipping values that have no data, so the spacing lies about the spread.
canonical_error.example: For the data 2, 3, 3, 5, 8, the student draws a number line labeled 2, 3, 5, 8 with equal gaps -- no 4, 6, or 7.
canonical_error.why: The student treats the axis as a list of the values that happen to appear instead of a true number line. Once the gaps are wrong, the shape of the data is wrong: 8 looks like the next-door neighbor of 5, and the display can no longer show clusters or gaps -- the whole reason it exists.

redirect_script.stop: Wait -- check your number line before adding Xs.
redirect_script.prompt: Read your axis out loud and count up by ones (or by your interval). Did you say every number from the minimum to the maximum, even the ones with no data? Empty values still get a tick -- they just get zero Xs.
redirect_script.praise: Your number line kept every value in place -- now the shape of the data is honest.

worked_example_script.text: Write the data on the board: 2, 3, 3, 5. Say: 'We're going to build the dot plot together, and then read how many Xs go above 3.'
What's the smallest value and the largest value? So what numbers does our number line need to reach?
Between 2 and 5, is there any value nobody picked? Should 4 still get a tick mark on the line?

This is THE error to catch. If the student writes the line as 2, 3, 5 with equal gaps -- skipping 4 -- stop: 'Your line says 3 and 5 are neighbors. Count the steps from 3 to 5. Where does 4 go?' Have them redraw with 2, 3, 4, 5, giving 4 a tick and zero Xs.
A number line is a ruler, not a guest list. Every value from 2 to 5 gets a tick; 4 just holds zero Xs.
Now place one X per data value. The number 3 appears twice in the list -- so how many Xs stack above 3?
Count all your Xs. How many should there be in the whole plot, and why?
Two Xs stack above 3, so the answer is 2. And four data values make four Xs total -- one above 2, two above 3, none above 4, one above 5 -- so the count check confirms nothing was dropped or doubled.

skills.name: Interpret histograms and box plots to judge statements about data
skills.i_do_script: A histogram's bars count STUDENTS; the axis counts HOURS -- and the median is an hours-number, not a bar height. Watch: bars of height 2, 6, 3, 1 over the intervals 0-4, 5-9, 10-14, 15-19. Is the median 6? No -- 6 is how many values sit in 5-9. There are 12 values, so the median is between the 6th and 7th values; counting in, both land in the 5-9 interval, so the median is somewhere between 5 and 9. On a box plot the same discipline applies: range is max minus min, IQR is Q3 minus Q1, and about half the data lives inside the box.

canonical_error.pattern: Reads the tallest bar's height as the median (or as 'the answer'), treating a frequency as if it were a data value.
canonical_error.example: Bars of height 2, 6, 3, 1 over intervals 0-4, 5-9, 10-14, 15-19 -- the student says 'the median is 6' because the tallest bar reaches 6.
canonical_error.why: The vertical axis counts how MANY values are in each interval; the median is a value from the horizontal axis. The student collapses the two axes into one, so any prominent number on the plot (usually the tallest bar's height) gets reported as the median. Finding the median actually requires counting to the middle value across the bars.

redirect_script.stop: Careful -- is 6 an amount, or a count of students?
redirect_script.prompt: Touch the vertical axis and say what it counts (students). Touch the horizontal axis and say what it measures (hours). The median is an HOURS number. Add up all the bars, find which interval holds the middle value, and answer with numbers from the bottom axis.
redirect_script.praise: You answered with a data value, not a bar height -- that's real interpretation.

skills.name: Compute the five-number summary and match data to its box plot
skills.i_do_script: Watch me build the five-number summary for 5, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 14. The data's already ordered -- always check that first. Median: the middle value is 9. Now the Indiana rule: when I split into halves to find the quartiles, the median itself sits out. Lower half 5, 7, 8 gives Q1 = 7; upper half 11, 12, 14 gives Q3 = 12. Five numbers -- 5, 7, 9, 12, 14 -- and that's exactly the box plot: whiskers at 5 and 14, box from 7 to 12, line at 9.

canonical_error.pattern: Includes the median in both halves (or one half) when splitting the data to find Q1 and Q3.
canonical_error.example: For 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, the student uses the lower half 3, 5, 6, 8 and gets Q1 = 5.5 instead of using 3, 5, 6 to get Q1 = 5.
canonical_error.why: The student knows quartiles come from 'halves' but hasn't internalized that the median is the CUT, not a member of either half (the convention this standard uses). Including it shifts both quartiles toward the middle, so the box is drawn too narrow and every IQR answer comes out wrong.

redirect_script.stop: Pause -- did the median sneak into your half?

redirect_script.praise: You benched the median before splitting -- your quartiles are trustworthy.

activities.title: Bench the Median
materials: Index cards numbered with a 7-value data set (e.g. 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14)
activities.instructions:
1. Groups lay their shuffled cards in a row, then order them least to greatest.
2. Find the median by removing one card from each end, back and forth. The last card standing is the median.
3. Place the median card on the BENCH square -- it sits out.
4. Find the middle of the left group (Q1) and the right group (Q3) the same crossing-off way.
5. Write the five-number summary and sketch the box plot above the cards.
6. Debrief: what would change if the benched card had joined a half? Try it and compare Q1s.

activities.title: Summary-to-Plot Match
activities.instructions:
1. Spread data cards and summary cards face up.
2. Pairs compute each data card's five-number summary and find its matching card.
3. One summary card is a decoy built by including the median in the halves -- it matches nothing.
4. Debrief: how did you catch the decoy? (Its quartiles are squeezed toward the median.)

strategy_links.why: Physically benching the median card makes the exclude-the-median convention concrete before it's symbolic.
The five-number procedure has crisp steps (order, median, bench, halves, quartiles) suited to gradual release.
Quick number talks on 'median of 3, 5, 6?' keep the middle-of-a-half computation automatic.

questioning_prompts: Is the data ordered? Prove it before anything else.
Which value is the median -- and which halves does it belong to?

skills.name: Draw and defend conclusions by comparing data displays
skills.i_do_script: Two box plots, one question: which class collected more cans? I don't guess from looks -- I pull numbers off the plots and put them in my sentence. Class A's median is 33 cans; Class B's is 28. And three-quarters of Class A's weeks were at 26 cans or more -- that's Class B's WORST week matching A's 25th percentile. So my claim is 'Class A collected more,' and my evidence is those two cited values. A claim without a number from the plot isn't a conclusion yet.

canonical_error.pattern: Reads a longer box or wider plot as 'more data' or 'a bigger total,' treating length as count.
canonical_error.example: Comparing Class A's box (spanning 26 to 40) with Class B's (27 to 29), the student says 'Class A has more data because its box is longer.'
canonical_error.why: Each section of a box plot holds about 25% of that data set no matter how long it looks -- length shows SPREAD, not how many values or how much total. The student maps 'bigger picture' to 'bigger amount,' which reverses many comparisons (a long box often means less consistency, not more of anything).

redirect_script.stop: Careful -- does longer mean MORE, or more SPREAD OUT?
redirect_script.prompt: Each chunk of a box plot -- whisker, box-half, box-half, whisker -- holds about 25% of that class's data, long or short. Compare the plots with numbers instead: read both medians, then both IQRs, and say what each one tells you.
redirect_script.praise: You cited actual values as evidence -- that's how a claim becomes a conclusion.

skills.item_template: One or two data displays (dot plots or box plots, 8-15 values or given summaries). Student makes or judges a claim and supports it with at least one value read from the display. Multi-part: Part A a computed value, Part B an evidence-based sentence. ER/MP with figure.

sample_items.stem: Two classes collected canned food for the same number of weeks. The box plots below show cans collected per week. One student claims Class A collected more cans overall; another claims Class B did. Part A: What is each class's median? Part B: Which student is correct? Support your conclusion with data from the plots.
sample_items.answer: Part A: Class A's median is 33 cans; Class B's median is 28 cans. Part B: The first student (Class A). A typical week for Class A (median 33) beats a typical week for Class B (median 28), and 75% of Class A's weeks were at 26 cans or more -- Class B's very best week was only 31.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students who reason 'B's box is tiny so B is worse at collecting' by luck, or 'A's box is longer so A has more' by the length-equals-count error, both need the median citation to be actually right.

sample_items.stem: The box plots below show points scored by two teams. Part A: Find each team's IQR. Part B: A coach says Team B is the more consistent team. Do the plots support the claim? Use data as evidence.
sample_items.answer: Part A: Team A's IQR is 34 - 24 = 10; Team B's IQR is 29 - 27 = 2. Part B: Yes. Both teams have the same median (28), but Team B's middle 50% spans only 2 points while Team A's spans 10, and B's full range (26 to 30) is far narrower than A's (20 to 40) -- B's scores are much more consistent.
sample_items.distractor_logic: The equal medians force students past 'which is bigger' into spread-based reasoning; the length-equals-more error picks Team A.

sample_items.stem: The dot plot below shows how many minutes 10 students take to walk to school. Part A: What are the range and median of the data? Part B: Jordan says 18 minutes is a typical walking time for this group. Use the plot to agree or disagree.
sample_items.answer: Part A: Range = 18 - 10 = 8; median = 12. Part B: Disagree. The value 18 appears once and sits 3 minutes beyond the next closest value (15); most of the data clusters from 10 to 15 and the median is 12, so 18 is one of the least typical times shown, not a typical one.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students anchored to the maximum, or to 'it's on the plot so it's typical,' fail to weigh where the data clusters.

worked_example_script.text: Project the two canned-food box plots: Class A (min 20, Q1 26, median 33, Q3 40, max 44) above Class B (min 26, Q1 27, median 28, Q3 29, max 31).
Just from looks -- which class seems like the bigger collector? Don't answer yet; tell me what your eye is reacting to.

If anyone says 'Class A has more data because its plot is longer,' pause there. Ask: 'If both classes collected for the same number of weeks, can one plot hold more weeks than the other?' Establish: every section of each plot is about 25% of THAT class's weeks. Length is spread, not amount.
Let's get real evidence. What is each class's median week?
33 versus 28 -- what does that comparison let us claim?
Find one MORE piece of evidence. Where does Class A's Q1 sit compared to Class B's whole plot?
A's Q1 is 26 -- so 75% of A's weeks beat or match B's worst week, and A's Q1 nearly matches B's minimum. Claim: Class A collected more. Evidence: median 33 vs 28, and Q1 26 vs max 31.
Now argue the other side for a second: what's the one thing Class B genuinely wins at? (Consistency -- IQR 2 vs 14.) A good conclusion knows what the other plot is better at.

practice_problems.stem: Leo compared the two box plots below and wrote the claim shown. Find the flaw in his reasoning and fix his conclusion.
shown_work: Leo wrote: 'Class A has more data than Class B
because Class A's box is way longer.'
practice_problems.answer: Box length shows SPREAD, not the amount of data -- each section of a box plot holds about 25% of that class's values no matter its length. practice_problems.stem: Using the canned-food box plots, which class collected more cans in a typical week? Cite at least one value from each plot.
practice_problems.answer: Class A. Its median week is 33 cans versus Class B's 28 -- and 75% of A's weeks were at 26 or more, while B never topped 31.

practice_problems.stem: Write one claim the two canned-food box plots DO support and one claim they do NOT let you make. Explain both.

practice_problems.stem: The histogram shows weekly exercise hours for 12 residents. The mayor claims 'most residents exercise at least 5 hours a week.' Does the histogram support the claim? Use counts as evidence.
practice_problems.answer: No. Only 3 + 1 = 4 of the 12 residents (one third) are at 5 or more hours; 8 of 12 are below 5. The data supports the opposite claim.

activities.title: Claim Court
materials: Projected pair of box plots (the canned-food pair)
activities.instructions:
1. Post the two box plots. Deal each group 4 claim slips (e.g. 'A's median is higher,' 'A has more weeks of data,' 'B is more consistent,' 'A collected 400 cans total').
2. Groups sort each claim under SUPPORTED or NOT SUPPORTED.
3. Rule: a SUPPORTED verdict must come with a cited value; a NOT SUPPORTED verdict must say what the plot can't show.
4. Groups present one verdict each; the class may overrule with better evidence.
5. Debrief: which claims failed because box plots hide counts and totals?

activities.title: Longer Box, More Stuff?
materials: Sketch of two box plots with equal medians, very different IQRs
activities.instructions:
1. Show two box plots with the same median: one box wide, one narrow.
2. Present the claim: 'The wide-box group has more data.'
3. Pairs must break the claim: what does each quarter of a box plot hold? (About 25% of its own data set.)
4. Pairs write the corrected comparison sentence using the word 'spread' or 'IQR.'
5. Debrief: when IS a wide box a bad sign? (When you want consistency.)

content.worked_problem: Team A box plot (20, 24, 28, 34, 40) vs Team B (26, 27, 28, 29, 30). Claim: 'Team A has more data because its box is longer.'
content.error_step: Treats box length as a count of data values instead of the spread of the middle 50%.
content.why: Every box plot section holds about a quarter of that data set regardless of length. Length measures spread: Team A's IQR is 10, Team B's is 2 -- same median, very different consistency, and no information about how many values either team has.

activities.title: Evidence Auction
activities.instructions:
1. Project a dot plot and a claim ('15 is a typical value here').
2. Each student writes ONE piece of evidence for or against the claim (a median, a cluster, a gap, a count) on scrap paper.
3. Collect and read bids aloud; the class ranks the three strongest.
4. Debrief: what made the winning evidence strong? (Specific values + where the data clusters.)

strategy_links.why: Claims and evidence are social -- Think-Pair-Share makes students defend a conclusion aloud before writing it.
Modeling a think-aloud ('my eye says A is bigger... but what NUMBER says so?') shows how to convert impressions into evidence.
A worked comparison next to the length-equals-count error sharpens what legitimate evidence looks like.

questioning_prompts: What's your claim -- and what NUMBER from the plot backs it up?
What does each quarter of a box plot hold, no matter how long it looks?
Both medians are equal -- so what should we compare instead?
What is one thing this display CANNOT tell us?
Argue the other side for a moment: what is the other group genuinely better at?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student says the group with the longer box or wider plot 'has more data' or 'collected more.'
misconception_redirects.say: Each chunk of a box plot -- whisker, box-half, box-half, whisker -- holds about 25% of that class's data, long or short. Compare the plots with numbers instead: read both medians, then both IQRs, and say what each one tells you.
misconception_redirects.praise: You cited actual values as evidence -- that's how a claim becomes a conclusion.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student makes a correct-sounding claim with no cited value ('A is obviously better').
misconception_redirects.say: In this room a claim needs a number. Read me one value from each plot -- a median, an IQR, a count -- and put both into your sentence: '___ because A's ___ is ___ and B's is ___.'
misconception_redirects.praise: Claim plus cited values -- that conclusion would hold up anywhere.

quick_checks.prompt: Two box plots, same median, box widths 2 and 10. Which group is more consistent, and how do you know?
quick_checks.look_for: The narrow-box group, citing IQR/spread. Picking the wide box 'because it's bigger' is the length-equals-more error resurfacing.

quick_checks.prompt: Can you tell from a box plot how many data values it summarizes? Yes or no, and why?
quick_checks.look_for: No -- it shows five summary values only. A 'yes' means the summary-vs-values distinction from S1/S2 needs revisiting.

worked_solution.stem: Team A's box plot: min 20, Q1 24, median 28, Q3 34, max 40. Team B's: min 26, Q1 27, median 28, Q3 29, max 30. A coach claims Team B is more consistent. Judge the claim with evidence.
worked_solution.answer: The claim is supported: Team B's IQR is 2 versus Team A's 10, and B's range is 4 versus A's 20, while the medians are equal.

steps.annotation: Start at the center. Equal medians mean 'typical' performance is the same -- so the claim must live or die on spread.
Consistency IS small spread. B's middle 50% fits in 2 points; A's needs 10.
The whisker-to-whisker check agrees. Two independent measures of spread both point the same way.

steps.math: Conclusion: the claim is supported -- B is more consistent (IQR 2 vs 10)
steps.annotation: Claim, plus cited values from BOTH plots. Box length here means spread -- not 'more data.'

faded_example.stem: Group A's box plot: min 10, Q1 14, median 18, Q3 22, max 26. Group B's: min 16, Q1 17, median 18, Q3 19, max 20. Which group is more consistent? Support your answer.
faded_example.answer: Group B: IQR 2 versus Group A's 8 (and range 4 versus 16), with equal medians of 18.

steps.math: Medians: A = 18, B = 18 -- centers are equal
steps.annotation: Compare centers first; here they tie, so spread decides.
Compute both IQRs (Q3 - Q1 for each group).
Write the conclusion: name the more consistent group AND cite the two IQRs as evidence.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S4 (interpret a box plot/histogram statement) -- the At-Proficiency center of the standard. If they pass, move up to S5 (compute the five-number summary) and S6 (defend conclusions). If they fail, drop to S2 (can they even read one value off a plot?) and S1 (do they know what each display shows?). S3 (create a plot) branches off S2 for students whose reads are fine but whose constructions collapse the axis. Foundation F1/F2 catch students who can't find a median or count occurrences at all.
